culture: Boleros (shoe shiners) work at a puesto, a small street stand, in Mexico
'Boleada' means a shoe shine
A bolero is a shoe shiner
'Grasa' is shoe polish (literally grease), in brown (café) or black (negro)
'Puesto' means a stand or stall
Shoe-shining is a trade often passed down from father to son
A bolero takes care of his tin of polish like a treasure; the tin can be a family heirloom
Shoe shiners clean off dust with a brush, apply polish with fingers, then buff with a cloth to a shine (brillo)
'Quedaron como espejos' means the shoes turned out like mirrors
The Roma is a neighborhood (colonia) in Mexico City where shoe shiners work
'Usted' is the polite form of address, used with customers and elders
'Joven' is a polite way to address a young man
Don is a respectful title used before the first name of an older man
'Platicar' means to chat, and friendly conversation is part of the service
'Café' means brown as a color
Common polite farewell: '¡Hasta luego, que le vaya muy bien!'

culture: Cempasúchil (marigold) is the flower traditionally used for Día de Muertos altars
The marigold's bright orange color and scent are believed to guide the dead back home
Families put up altars (ofrendas) in their homes for Día de Muertos
Marigolds are sold fresh in bunches (manojos) at the market
Marigold petals or flowers are laid in a path on the floor leading to the door so the dead can follow it
Two bunches of marigold is enough to make a home altar look nice
Flowers are tied up carefully (amarraditos) so they don't get damaged in transit
Día de Muertos has a distinctive marigold smell that fills the house
Marigold wreaths (coronas de cempasúchil) are made for Día de Muertos
Vendors often cut flowers early in the morning and bring them to market the same day
Market stalls (puestos) are a common place to buy flowers
Mexicans use diminutives like fresquecito, llenitos and amarraditos to sound warm and friendly
Vendors greet customers with 'pase, pase' to invite them into the stall
Marigold bunches cost around thirty pesos
'Platicar' is the Mexican word for chatting
